chief_complaint: straining to void, splayed bifid urine stream, and incomplete emptying months after straddle injury
hpi_details: 41M status post bicycle crossbar straddle injury one year ago with severe obstructive voiding, Qmax under 8 mL/sec, and a RUG-confirmed 2.5 cm bulbar urethral stricture. He needs reconstructive-urology assessment to discuss durable management options.
ideas: He thinks his prostate was badly bruised when he slammed onto the bicycle crossbar and never healed properly.
concerns: He is worried that his urine flow will shut down completely while he is on a construction job site and require an emergency catheter.
expectations: He hopes to discuss a procedure that can open up the narrowed channel so he can empty his bladder with a steady stream again.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Urethral Stricture Obstructive Voiding evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Urethral Stricture Obstructive Voiding is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Treatment is selected by stricture length, location, etiology, tissue quality, prior procedures, and patient goals; a 2.5 cm bulbar stricture does not automatically require a buccal mucosa graft.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: straining to void, splayed bifid urine stream, and incomplete emptying months after straddle injury
Key HPI features: remote straddle injury, obstructive lower urinary tract symptoms, low flow, and a 2.5 cm bulbar stricture on RUG.

Objective/Exam findings: Record uroflowmetry pattern and post-void residual; obtain urinalysis/culture when infection is suspected and define length/location with RUG, with VCUG or cystoscopy when needed for operative planning.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Urethral Stricture Obstructive Voiding.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Urinary tract infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Repeated blind urethral catheter attempts in retention when a stricture is known or suspected, risking false passage and injury.
Missing infected obstruction, renal impairment, or acute retention requiring urgent decompression.
management_principles: Refer to reconstructive urology for shared decision-making. A single endoscopic treatment may be considered for selected short bulbar strictures, but repeated dilation or urethrotomy has poor durability.
Discuss urethroplasty options based on anatomy, including excision and primary anastomosis or substitution/augmentation with oral mucosa when appropriate.
If retention occurs, obtain urgent urologic help for safe drainage (guidewire-assisted catheterization or suprapubic diversion as appropriate) rather than repeated blind attempts.
Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 41M with obstructive voiding one year after straddle injury; Qmax is under 8 mL/sec and RUG shows a 2.5 cm bulbar stricture. Ask about retention, infection, hematuria, prior instrumentation, and erectile function.
reference_soap.objective: Review RUG and obtain uroflowmetry/post-void residual; use urinalysis/culture if infection is suspected and add VCUG or cystoscopy if required for operative planning.
reference_soap.assessment: Post-traumatic 2.5 cm bulbar urethral stricture causing bothersome bladder-outlet obstruction.
reference_soap.plan: Refer to reconstructive urology to select endoscopic versus urethroplasty management based on full anatomy and prior treatment; avoid repeated endoscopic procedures when durable reconstruction is appropriate. Send for urgent assessment for retention, systemic infection, or reduced urine output; avoid repeated blind catheter attempts.

Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for urology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: Urology evaluation for patient presenting with straining to void, splayed bifid urine stream, and incomplete emptying months after straddle injury.
red_flags: Inability to pass urine, worsening suprapubic pain/distension, or very low urine output (urgent decompression assessment)
Fever, rigors, flank pain, or confusion with obstructive urinary symptoms (possible infected obstruction)

must_ask.objective: History of straddle injury or urethral trauma
must_ask.say: Did you have any injury to your groin or pelvis, like a fall onto a bicycle crossbar, before these symptoms began?
Has your urine stream become weak, split into two streams, or sprayed instead of a single stream?
Do you have to strain to start or keep urinating, and does it feel like your bladder is not completely empty afterward?

must_ask.objective: History of urethral catheterization or instrumentation
must_ask.say: Have you ever had a urinary catheter placed, or any prior surgery or scope procedure on your urethra?
Have you had repeated urinary tract infections since this started?

history.answer: My urine stream has become very weak and keeps splitting in two, and I have to push hard just to get it out.
My main problem is difficulty passing urine. I am not having issues with involuntary leaking or accidents.
It started gradually about eight or nine months ago, several months after a bicycle accident, and it has become steadily worse over time.
The stream is very slow, sprays out, and often splits into two separate streams. It also takes me a few seconds of waiting before the flow starts.
I have to bear down and strain my abdominal muscles the whole time, and the stream repeatedly stops and starts before I finish.
I never feel like my bladder is completely empty when I finish, and urine keeps dribbling into my underwear for a minute afterward.
I can still pass urine every time I try, so it has not shut off completely, but my lower belly feels uncomfortably full.
I go to the bathroom around eight to ten times during the day, and I have to get up two or three times every night to urinate.
I feel a sudden strong urge when my bladder is full, but I can hold it and I have never leaked on my way to the bathroom.
No, I never leak urine when I cough, sneeze, laugh, or lift heavy weights at the gym.
Taking so long in the bathroom is very frustrating and disrupts my work day, but I do not need to wear any pads or protective underwear.
I do not have any burning or pain when I pass urine, and I have never noticed any pink or red discoloration in my urine.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
No, I have never had a diagnosed bladder or kidney infection.
I have no lower back pain, no leg weakness or numbness, no numbness around my groin or buttocks, and no difficulty controlling my bowels.
My bowel movements are regular once a day, and I do not suffer from constipation.
I drink about four or five glasses of water a day and one cup of black coffee in the morning, and I limit fluids before going to bed.
No, I have not taken any cold medications, allergy pills, decongestants, antidepressants, or water pills.
About a year ago, my foot slipped off the pedal and I fell hard directly onto the horizontal crossbar of my bicycle. It caused severe perineal bruising and pain that took several weeks to clear up.
No, I have never had a urinary catheter placed, and I have never undergone any cystoscopy or procedures inside my urethra.
No, I have never had urethritis, urethral discharge, or any sexually transmitted infections.
My erections and sexual function have been completely normal, and I do not have pain with ejaculation.
I do not have any chronic medical conditions like diabetes, high blood pressure, stroke, or Parkinson's disease.
I have never had any surgeries and I have never been hospitalized.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or vitamins.
I have no known allergies to any medicines, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I drink alcohol only occasionally, maybe one or two beers a month at social gatherings.
I work as an office manager and live with my wife. Outside of work, I lead an active lifestyle and enjoy cycling and running.
My father had mild prostate enlargement in his late sixties, but there is no family history of prostate cancer, kidney problems, or urethral strictures.

I figured that bike wreck bruised my prostate so badly that it swelled up and pinched the passage shut. I'm afraid my bladder is going to shut down completely while I'm at work and I'll end up rushed to the ER for a catheter.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.7°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Well-appearing, athletic male sitting comfortably, in no visible distress.
Abdomen is flat with no surgical scars, rashes, or visible masses.
Abdomen is soft and non-tender; mild, non-painful fullness palpable in the suprapubic area with no guarding or rebound tenderness.
Dullness to percussion extending approximately 3 cm above the pubic symphysis, indicating moderate bladder fullness.
No tenderness elicited on percussion over either costovertebral angle.
Normal circumcised phallus without meatal narrowing or discharge; faint induration palpable along the ventral bulbar urethra without focal tenderness.
Normal resting sphincter tone; smooth, symmetric, non-tender prostate of normal size (approximately 20 grams) with no palpable nodules.
Normal muscle bulk and 5/5 motor strength symmetrically throughout both lower extremities.
Intact light touch and sharp sensation across lower extremity dermatomes and the perineal saddle area.
Symmetric 2+ patellar and Achilles deep tendon reflexes bilaterally; negative Babinski sign.
